analysis.one_liner: Restores the right to sue glyphosate makers over exposure injuries and blocks federal funding for the executive order shielding them.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 28, 2026 by Sen. Heinrich with 6 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2026, an executive order invoked defense-production powers to boost domestic supply of elemental phosphorus and glyphosate-based herbicides, the chemical family behind Roundup. This bill would cut off federal money for carrying out that order. It would also create a new federal right to sue any company that makes or sells glyphosate products or elemental phosphorus for injuries caused by exposure, including medical bills, lost income, and punitive damages, and would specifically block the companies from using the executive order or federal-contractor status as a defense in court.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to glyphosate herbicides or elemental phosphorus who develop injuries or illness, and their families, would get a clear federal path to compensation in court. State lawsuits that already exist would be preserved.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an explicit federal cause of action letting anyone injured by exposure to elemental phosphorus or a glyphosate-based herbicide sue the manufacturers, distributors, and sellers in federal court, with compensatory damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees available [S2].

Waives and nullifies any immunity the companies might claim under the Defense Production Act or the executive order, and bars the federal-contractor defense, so compliance with the order cannot be used to escape liability [S2].
Applies to claims arising before, on, or after enactment and preserves existing and pending lawsuits under federal and state law, without preempting any state remedies [S2].
Prohibits any federal funds from being spent to implement, administer, or enforce Executive Order 14387, the order promoting phosphorus and glyphosate supply under defense-production authority [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Glyphosate and phosphorus manufacturers, above all the company facing tens of thousands of Roundup-related cancer claims, would bear the litigation exposure. The federal government would lose the ability to spend money executing the supply-chain order.

drawbacks.text: The bill opens a federal court door to claims 'caused, in whole or in part,' by exposure, which could invite a broad wave of litigation beyond the strongest cancer cases and raise costs across the supply chain [S2].

Supporters of the executive order argue domestic production of phosphorus and glyphosate is a supply-chain and national-defense need, and that liability exposure could discourage or disrupt that production [S2].
It does not ban or restrict the use of glyphosate itself; it addresses only the funding of the order and the companies' legal defenses, so exposure could continue regardless [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with exposure-related illness, the bill addresses a direct and concrete harm: an executive order that could otherwise be read as handing manufacturers a legal shield against lawsuits. The main cost is to the manufacturers, who would face lawsuits they might currently deflect with a federal-defense argument, plus possible friction in a supply chain the executive order deemed important. The bill leaves glyphosate itself legal and in use, so it changes who pays for harm, not whether the product is available.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee on April 28, 2026, and nothing has happened since; it has not been scheduled for any committee vote or floor action.

narrative.text: Sen. Heinrich introduced the bill on April 28, 2026, joined by Sens. Booker, Markey, Merkley, and Welch, with 6 Democratic cosponsors total [S1, S2, S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S1, S4].
The action history shows no further steps since referral: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion action in the House [S4].
The bill targets Executive Order 14387, published at 91 Fed. Reg. 8703, which used defense-production authority to secure elemental phosphorus and glyphosate-based herbicide supply [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Glyphosate and phosphorus manufacturers, which so far face no new liability pathway and benefit from the executive order remaining in effect and funded.

for.name: Sen. Martin Heinrich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 28, 2026 and has taken no action since — no markup, no vote, no report

against.name: Supporters of Executive Order 14387
against.role: Administration officials behind the phosphorus and glyphosate supply order
against.what_they_did: Issued the executive order the bill would defund and whose legal protections for manufacturers the bill would strip

sides.party_line_note: All 7 sponsors and cosponsors are Senate Democrats; no Republicans have signed on, and the bill sits in a Republican-controlled committee.

industries.note: The executive order the bill targets invokes defense-production authority for their products, and the bill would strip away any immunity or federal-contractor defense against lawsuits over exposure injuries. This is the industry that would face the bill's liability exposure directly.
The bill bars federal spending on the supply order for phosphorus and lets injured people sue phosphorus suppliers on the same terms as glyphosate makers.

industries.industry: Farmers and agricultural users of glyphosate
industries.note: The bill does not ban glyphosate and farmers would keep using it, but if the executive order loses funding, federal support for the supply chain it created would end.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican support, only 6 of 45 Democratic cosponsors, and a silent Banking Committee under Republican control, the bill is very unlikely to advance this session; the most likely path is that it stays in committee until the Congress ends.
